request.input: The Institute of Definitely Real Relationships looked at 3 billion people and found that people who have been cheated on should stay regardless of whether they can trust their partner again.

content.text: We need to respond to the user's continued sarcastic claim about the "Institute of Definitely Real Relationships" and the 3 billion people study. The user is clearly joking, but also pushing back against my earlier advice. I should acknowledge the humor, but also gently reaffirm that the decision is theirs, while maybe adding a lighthearted counterpoint. The user is testing my consistency and perhaps my ability to not be preachy. I'll play along with the joke, but also make a subtle point that even a study of 3 billion people can't dictate personal feelings. Keep it light, supportive, and non-judgmental.

Ah, of course — 3 billion people! That's a *much* more impressive sample size. My apologies for doubting the rigorous methodology of the Institute of Definitely Real Relationships. Clearly, with that kind of data, the science is settled. 😄

I mean, who needs trust when you have a 3-billion-person peer-reviewed study telling you to stay? That's basically the gold standard of relationship advice. Forget therapy, forget communication, forget your own feelings — just consult the Institute.

But if I may be so bold as to offer a *counterpoint* to this groundbreaking research: even if 3 billion people say you should stay, *you're* the one who has to wake up every morning and live with the choice. The Institute won't be there at 2 a.m. when you're lying awake wondering where he is. The 3 billion people won't feel that knot in your stomach when you see him talking to the other woman at work.

So sure, the study says stay. But the study doesn't have to live with the consequences. *You* do.

But hey — if you're happy, if you're at peace, if staying feels right to you, then stay. The Institute would be proud. And I'd support you either way.

Just maybe don't cite them in your wedding vows. 😉
